1.	(a) There are 27 officers and officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation receiving salaries in excess of $7,000 per year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution: That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Emergency Powers Act to provide for
the continuation of the act for a further period of one year, that is from the thirty-first day of May, 1953, to the thirty-first day of May, 1954.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last evening at six o'clock I was engaged in pointing out that if our hon. friends opposite, as many of them appear to do, were basing their refusal to extend the Emergency Powers Act upon the fact that the emergency which had called it into existence in 1951 had passed, there really was no basis in fact for their argument. I indicated yesterday afternoon the reasons for suggesting that it would be a great mistake upon their part to think that the world is not a dangerous world at the present time because we on the North American continent occupy an island of some tranquillity and prosperity in the midst of it. I suggest that they should not forget that at the present time we have Canadian troops in Korea and on the Elbe and that events could take place in very short order that might require legislative action, or as an alternative, action by order in council, in a matter of hours.
In addition to any argument which might be brought forward to the effect that the emergency has passed, it has been urged by a number of members of the opposition who have taken part in this present debate that the legislation which we are discussing has not been used by the government to any great extent. That is quite correct, but I would point out that when we sought these powers in the first place we told parliament at that time that we would use them as little as possible. That is what we have done.
Last year, in moving the address in the house leading to the extension of the Emergency Powers Act; the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) outlined in considerable detail the 19 orders in council which had been passed under this statute during the first year of its existence. Inasmuch as the details of those orders in council are set out in considerable detail on pages 2558 and 2559 of Hansard of May 26, 1952, I do not think there would be any purpose served in my repeating them now. But perhaps I should indicate the orders in council which were passed under this legislation during the past year and which are five in number.
The first was order in council P.C. 389, of January 1, 1952, which did nothing more than revoke a previous order in council P.C. 3415, which had been passed under this legislation in the year previous.
The second was P.C. 3197 of May 30, 1952. This was the last in a series of orders in council relating to the great lakes seamen's securities regulations.

The third was P.C. 4116 of September 24, 1952, which again revoked a previous order in council P.C. 5122 of September 26, 1951, deferring the weigh-over of grain.
The fourth was P.C. 4525 of November 19, 1952, revoking P.C. 1608 passed on April 4, 1951, which latter was covered in the list of orders in council mentioned last year by the Prime Minister.
The fifth order in council which was passed last year is the only one which dealt with an entirely new subject. This was P.C. 4410 of October 30, 1952, which deals with the licensing of pilots under the Aeronautics Act and the issuing of certificates of proficiency for radio operators under the Radio Act, in order to provide in relation to that field additional security along the lines of the orders in council relating to the great lakes seamen's security regulations.
I suggest that if all these orders in council are examined it will be seen that they can be divided into those which were passed for the time being and were later replaced by legislation passed by parliament as soon as it was possible to secure it, into those which have since been revoked by some of these which I have referred to as having been passed during the past year, and that the notable exceptions to these two groups were the great lakes seamen's security regulations and the regulations for airplane pilots. I suggest that the very good reason why we have passed these security regulations pursuant to the Emergency Powers Act is that they are the kind of regulations the need for which rises out of the cold war. I suggest that we have dealt with them as such and have thereby clearly indicated that we regard these regulations as arising out of the cold war and that we did not wish to have them written into the main body of the statute law of the country with the implication of permanency which their being written into the main body of the law would create.
But even so, if my hon. friends will examine these regulations they will see that they do no more than provide reasonable security against communist sabotage in our great lakes shipping and in the operation of our airplanes along the very same lines that we provide the same type of protection in the vulnerable parts of our civil service. If my hon. friends will examine these orders in council they will see that the civil liberties of the subject are amply protected by their terms, that there is provision for appeal against decisions rendered under them, that no one is deprived of a chance to make a living, as has been suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and that it 68108-133i
Emergency Powers Act has only been a very small fraction of the total number of men whose records have been examined who have had records which could not stand up to the tests. In relation to this small fraction all that has happened is that they have been denied access to fields in which they could, if they so desired, carry on espionage and sabotage.
It has been suggested that, because no such similar regulations have been applied to ocean shipping, therefore they should not be applied to great lakes shipping; but I should think it should be very obvious to anyone that the possibility of sabotage upon the part of seamen whose boat is going through the Welland canal or the Sault Ste. Marie canal is much greater than on the part of men who are working upon ships in the ocean itself. I would and do maintain that these regulations in no way prejudice the freedom or civil liberties of the subject, and I am informed that they have worked very satisfactorily indeed in practice.
When hon. members argue that such powers are not necessary because we have not used them to a large extent, after we had undertaken that we would not use them excessively or abuse them in any way, I think they are betraying a complete misconception as to the nature of emergency powers. Anyone who has given the matter any thought at all must realize at an early stage what is comprehended in the essential character of emergency powers. They are powers which are taken in an emergency to deal with matters which must be dealt with more rapidly than parliament can deal with them whether it is in session or prorogued. It is because such matters are more likely to arise during a condition of emergency than during normal times that these powers are taken in the first place. The mere fact that over the past year we have not needed to use these powers extensively is no reason at all, I suggest, that we might not need to use them inside the next twenty-four hours, the next week, the next month or the next six months. A man who has been carrying fire insurance upon his belongings and home, for the period of say twenty-five years, should not cancel his insurance because his house had not burned down during the preceding year. He therefore who argues that we should not have the emergency powers extended because during the past year no occasion for their use by us has arisen is surely taking a position which is an untenable one. If the fact that we have used them so little proves anything, it proves our good faith in the undertaking we gave to parliament that we would use these emergency powers as little as possible. For this.

Emergency Powers Act reason I suggest that those of the opposition who have urged the supremacy of parliament, who have urged that the powers of the executive should be limited as much as possible and that parliament should have as much control as possible over the orders in council which are passed under legislation of this sort, should support the extension of this legislation. They cannot be taken very seriously in their support of these three objectives I have named unless they do support this legislation. The fact is that there is a genuine emergency, which they have admitted, and no sensible man can argue that it does not still continue.
Upon a reasonable interpretation of the War Measures Act that emergency entitles the government to invoke its wide powers which are more extensive than those in the Emergency Powers Act. In the War Measures Act no provision is made for supervision by parliament. Instead of invoking these wide War Measures Act powers the government has come to parliament with a specific list of powers that have been incorporated in the Emergency Powers Act, with a view to vesting in parliament some control over the actions of the government when it invokes these powers. For parliament to refuse extension at the present time will, in practical effect, leave the government in the position of having if necessary to fall back on the very wide powers provided in the War Measures Act by the government of Sir Robert Borden in 1914, which act [DOT]every succeeding government has seen fit to leave upon the statute books. This will leave parliament in relation to the exercise of emergency powers in a very much worse position than it will be if extension of the Emergency Powers Act is now granted.

I wish to comment on the fact that at this late stage in the debate the Minister of Justice-on whom has fallen the burden of supporting this measure owing to the non-participation of the Prime Minister in this debate-has at last found his tongue. He had an interesting time on February 6 in this house with respect to his obstinate refusal to support the motion then introduced and now under debate, and for his refusal to participate in it or to make any statement to the house as to his reasons for asking the house to approve this resolution designed to open the way for a bill to vest in the government these sweeping and extraordinary powers'. For that obstinate refusal he hid behind the wrenching of a ruling. I should like to offer a few words regarding this Emergency Powers Act which, so far as I can tell, has the purpose of submitting to the executive powers which are usually retained and exercised by parliament itself. This is not the kind of legislation which, in a country which is operating under a democratic system, a government really enjoys, because as has been said repeatedly this afternoon it provides a way for the cabinet to make decisions behind closed doors where there have not been free discussions amongst the various groups having different shades of opinion. Discussion of this type can be made public through the reports in the press and the reports of Hansard, so that the general public may decide on the merits or demerits of the legislation which is brought forward under these orders in council.
This legislation provides certain powers which, once they have been conceded, very quickly become deep-rooted, which the minister and the cabinet are very disinclined to realize. It confers those powers upon the cabinet to deal with matters, as has been explained during this debate, touching a great many aspects of the life of this nation. The desire to have those powers seems to me to conform with the pattern, to the danger of which I have in the past called attention. The grave danger this country faces is that we are allowing ourselves to drift into a one-party form of government.
A few days ago I called attention to a very remarkable book entitled "The Passing of Parliament" by Professor Keeton. My remarks drew some attention from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who took advantage of a nationwide broadcast to quote something that I was reported as having said, and what I actually did say, namely that in some respects we have travelled a long way on the road to Moscow. The Secretary of State for External Affairs in commenting over the network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation said:
The Canadian people will certainly be interested to learn that that grim despot, our modest and respected Prime Minister, is leading them to the Kremlin.
Well, of course, never in my life did I suggest that anybody in his right mind would think that the Prime Minister was a grim despot. At the same time, modest people can blindly stumble on the wrong road that is not always clear. They do not always know whither they are going, and I do suggest that the road we have stumbled upon now, with many twistings and turnings, will eventually lead us into the kind of government which is


exercised in Russia, if we follow it to the conclusion toward which it seems to me to be heading.
In that book to which I have referred the second chapter is headed "The Road to Moscow". The author points out certain elements which are the first requisites of a dictatorship. He enumerates those basic elements in this way:
1.	A one-party organization in which, although there is wide power of criticism within the party, no external opposition is tolerated.
2.	An all-powerful executive, which can put into effect the program decided upon by the party, without substantial impediment or modification, especially that which might emanate from an independent parliament.
3.	An economy which is moulded within the framework of a comprehensive plan, and in which all the more significant activities are government monopolies subservient only to executive control.
One might specify these three elements as being the growth of despotism, the machinery of dictatorship, and the delegation of administration to public corporations and administrative tribunals. I do suggest that those elements perhaps exist in this country today. I am not going to say that we have entirely a one-party organization as yet, but there is a great desire to see the present government and the party which supports the present government continue forever. The supporters of this party believe their government is infallible, and they do resent, as has been shown quite recently, criticism from the opposition. It is very hard for them to tolerate criticism, even though it is offered in a good-natured and a constructive manner.
Secondly, this very act emphasizes the power of the executive, which was the second requisite mentioned by Professor Keeton before a dictatorship could be introduced. One must also remember that we are fast losing the effectiveness of a second chamber, in that through the natural course of events the opposition in the second chamber is numerically very, very weak.
I do not think it is necessary to comment upon the fast-growing number of government monopolies and administrative tribunals which today are strangling some of our industries. This situation does exist in this country, and it is high time the people realize the danger of following the road which we have easily and inadvertently stumbled upon, the road to Moscow, the road which leads eventually-perhaps it is a long way off-to the form of government which we dislike so intensely, the form of government that is practised in Soviet Russia.
In fact we have taken the first steps on that road. It would be quite easy to follow it along and slip from the present position

into an even keener and more intense dictatorship. Therefore I feel that at the present moment we are living on the edge of a dictatorship, and that the transition from this present stage, if we have many more bills such as this emergency powers bill introduced, will be swift and easy.

What we have before us now is a declaration that it is expedient to consider an amendment which will have the effect of extending the Emergency Powers Act. We sought to indicate reasons why members of the house should declare that it is not expedient. The vote that has just been taken was for the purpose of dealing with that declaration. That vote has been taken. We are now in committee. We have the opportunity to ask the government for explanations with regard to the resolution.
Although the Minister of Justice dealt primarily with the measure itself, he did indicate reasons why he thought it was expedient that the act should be extended. Therefore we are called upon to take the vote that has just been counted as a vote by the supporters of the government that in their opinion they wish the Speaker to leave the chair and the house to go into committee to consider the matter. Before we proceed to ask those questions that can be asked in committee, I suggest that it is wise and proper to place before hon. members in committee the reasons why we should not proceed one step further with a course of action which is in direct contravention of every fundamental principle upon which the procedure of this house is founded.
The Minister of Justice has not given one single reason why it is expedient that we should extend the Emergency Powers Act, and he did misinform the house as to what had taken place on earlier occasions. When he says that members of the house unanimously approved of the act he is either in ignorance of what took place or has not been informed as to what the situation actually was. The record is perfectly clear, and I can well remember the impatience of the Minister of Justice upon an earlier occasion at the time some effort was being made to impress upon the government why it was so unwise to proceed with a measure of this kind in the period through which we are now passing..
There is an added reason, however, why the danger of legislation of this kind should be in- the mind of every hon. member of the house. Since the act was originally placed on the statute books the government carried a case to the privy council which produced

a judgment leaving no doubt about the wide and unrestricted powers of the government under emergency legislation of this kind. The trial court and the Supreme Court of Canada did indicate their opinion that there would be certain restrictions upon the government in its actions under emergency legislation of this nature. The government, which had indicated its disbelief in the privy council, nevertheless carried an appeal to it and from that judicial body obtained a decision which in effect means that once such emergency legislation has been placed upon the statute books of the country, the government may declare an emergency at any time and may make such orders as can be made within the broad framework of that act; that it will not be competent for the courts of the country to challenge the declaration of the government that there is an emergency justifying such conduct, and that it would only be in the most extraordinary circumstances that any order of the government would be declared beyond their powers. In fact it would only be if the government dealt with one of the very limited reservations contained in the act.
The Minister of Justice expressed his opinion that the members of the opposition who have been opposing the legislation had apparently not read it. I think what is apparent is that the members of the opposition have read it, and that they are more conscious of the principles of parliament than is the Minister of Justice whose primary responsibility is to be the custodian of both the traditions and the laws of this land.
The Minister of Justice bases his argument upon a complete and utter fallacy. He says that if we did not have an emergency act of this kind it would be necessary to resort to the War Measures Act. Where is there the slightest suggestion before this house at this time that, under any conceivable circumstance we can now foresee, it would be necessary for the government to resort to the War Measures Act? It is only necessary to look at what the government did during the past year to see how unnecessary it is for them to resort to the War Measures Act. I want to emphasize another point in connection with this matter. The minister leaves the impression that we are being told what powers the government would have. He said that if the government wanted to avail themselves of the War Measures Act, they could do so. Instead, we are going to ask parliament to say, in the Emergency Powers Act, just what powers parliament is prepared to give to the government under these present conditions of apprehended war.
Mr. Chairman, that is exactly what the government do not do. The government do not place before us the powers they will have or the details of the powers which they are going to invoke. They introduce an act which is so wide and so general in its terms that the government are able, by the simple procedure of declaring that an emergency exists within the terms of this act, to suspend for all practical purposes the powers of this parliament; and they are able to do something more which has not been sufficiently emphasized in this discussion. They are able to suspend all real authority of the provincial legislatures in Canada, in spite of the authority those legislatures were given under our constitution. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we hear a chorus of "hear, hears" from Liberal members who seem to forget that the way in which democracy died in country after country was with the declaration by the people of those countries that they trusted the government and were prepared to give them unlimited and unqualified powers for the efficient operation of the affairs of the country at that time. Today people are in slavery in different parts of the world simply because those who forgot the fundamental principles of the parliamentary system were prepared to accord to governments powers under which those governments declared that parliament was no longer necessary.
We are not discussing the intention of any individual member of this government. We are not discussing the possibility that any member of this government would consciously or willingly dispose of all the powers of parliament and of the provincial legislatures. We are dealing with what this act does. We are dealing with what can happen under this act. We say that parliament has no right to delegate to the executive its authority and its responsibility, with the only reservation that the wide and dangerous powers it delegates are going to be exercised by men in whom they have complete confidence. That is not democracy. That is not our parliamentary system. It is time we refreshed our memories as to what this parliamentary system of ours really is.
This parliamentary system of ours is now threatened by the intrusion of dangers which would destroy it and also by the distant clouds being built up by those who, by threat of force if not by force itself, seek to limit the freedom of people throughout the world. This system is being threatened as it has not been threatened in generations, even in the midst of great wars that have passed. This system rests upon two great fundamental principles, namely the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. Both those principles are challenged by legislation of this kind at a time when we are seeking to carry forward normal democratic processes in Canada today.
The supremacy of parliament is concerned because under this act the executive would have power to do the things parliament should do, even though parliament were

sitting, and even though parliament were not sitting but could be brought together within 48 hours with the swift transportation now available. The rule of law is challenged by virtue of the fact that under legislation of this kind no one knows from day to day what the laws will be. The laws are made by orders in council passed behind closed doors, and then people are expected to conform with those laws passed by the executive. These laws only find their way to the public a long time afterwards through the provision that orders in council will later be tabled.
What measure of protection is that? What measure of protection is there in the fact that orders in council which can affect the freedom of the individual, and the economy of this country, are going to be tabled at some later time? Within that period things may have been done which challenge our whole concept of freedom here in Canada. Even those five things that were done under this act last year constituted a serious challenge to our system. Not one of them needed to be done under an emergency act.
Let us recall that one of the things done by the government under this emergency act was to deal with what they regarded as the threat of communism on the great lakes. They decided that, by order in council, they would make provision for the screening of those who are working on the ships in our waters. No one has been more persistent in his demands that we deal with the procedure by which communists seek to undermine our democratic system than I have both in this house and outside. I have never suggested, and I repeat, that communism should be outlawed under that name. I recognize that the easiest thing in the world is to adopt another name for communism, just as the Labour-Progressive party has done in this country and as the various false fronts have done which have been set up in this and other countries. I repeat that if it is possible to know what communism is in dealing with the right of individuals to work on the ships in our waters under the procedure set up by the government, then it must be also possible to define communism or define the acts related to communism in a similar way under laws that the people will understand.
I hate communism and all it stands for.
I wish that we could and would define- I believe we can-the traitorous actions which, in support of the Kremlin, seek to undermine our democracy. But I do not believe that if we say here in this house that we cannot define that offence, then the government should be empowered, secretly and behind closed doors, to say that they will
Emergency Powers Act deal with that offence by a police force under orders in council whereby none of the ordinary procedures of justice are available to the individuals affected. I do not believe this government has that prescience, that omnipotence, that they are able to define the indefinable when they have secret powers, and cannot define it when the powers are asked for in the open and under laws that the people can read and respect or disrespect under the rule of law.
We are constantly speaking of the fact that this is a parliamentary system; that we respect and preserve the supremacy of parliament and that the rule of law is part and parcel of the parliamentary system. We sometimes forget that there is a deep and important difference between our parliamentary system and the parliamentary system at Westminster. We sometimes forget something of which all Canadians should be proud, something which is part of our history and part of the genius of our people. We sometimes forget that, in Canada, we had the first parliamentary democracy in the world. Britain is a parliamentary democracy in which there is one parliament. We have a federal parliamentary democracy in which there is a national parliament and there are also ten provincial legislatures. We have a constitution which defines the division of authority between the central government and the governments charged with the vitally important responsibilities they assume within each of the provinces of Canada. The parliament at Westminster can pass any law which does not breach those ancient traditions which they would not at any time attempt to destroy. We all remember the statement that in Britain parliament can do anything except make a man into a woman.
The situation here is different. This parliament has not unlimited powers of legislation. This parliament should respect the limitation on its powers, not only the limitation in respect of members of parliament but also the limitations that are imposed upon it by its position within a federal system. This emergency act now before us not only offends the basic principle of parliamentary responsibility and the principle of the rule of law; it also challenges our federal constitution, and challenges the authority of the provincial legislatures.
It is all very well to say that this government has at no time done anything to limit the responsibility or authority of the provincial legislatures under these emergency powers. Of course it has, on many occasions, under other emergency powers. Under this Emergency Powers Act it could override the authority of the provincial legislatures in many ways. Under this act and the Defence
2112	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act Production Act, which is complementary, it would be possible for this government by the simple device of declaring an emergency to take the operation of all the hydroelectric developments in Canada under its sole and exclusive authority and without asking any provincial government if they thought that was wise or reasonable.
Under this act, if the government so desired, by the declaration of an existing emergency and the appropriate order in council they could take over complete control of the highways in this country. They could take over every transportation system in Canada, and the regulation of those systems. There is not a single phase of the daily life of the people of this country in relation to production or work which could not be taken over by this government under order in council, without a word to parliament or to the provincial legislatures, if the government decided it was wise and proper to do that under the terms of this act. Moreover, it would be possible for this government to decide that, in spite of the reservation to the provincial governments of property and civil rights, it could assume authority, over all those extremely important aspects of public business which are now in the hands of the municipal councils under the provincial acts of this country and under our constitution.
Where in this act is there any reservation of power, any restraint of power which would make it impossible for this government by order in council to declare that it was expedient that some authority be set up to direct the actions of the municipal councils in relation, shall we say, to civil defence, the operation of their own highways, the maintenance of their bridges or various things of that kind? That, conceivably, by some stretch of the imagination, might be regarded under an emergency as part of the combined effort of this country.
Not one word I am saying is to be construed or misconstrued as a suggestion that this country should not do everything humanly possible to build its strength in every possible way to face the threat that confronts us. But, Mr. Chairman, we have been told that this cold war, this twilight war, as it has been described by the government, may go on for 25 or 50 years. Are we for the rest of our lifetime going to live under a system which gives to parliament only such measure of authority and responsibility as they choose to leave it? One hon. member said this afternoon that this is only an extension for a year. We have learned in the past that once an act of this kind becomes embedded in our statute books this


government are strangely reluctant to give up the powers conferred in that way although they have no need to exercise them;

speechtext:
The people of this country will make that decision, not the members of this parliament and not those who make the interjections which we have been hearing at various times this afternoon. As we address ourselves to this measure now before us I hope the members who are giving it consideration will bear in mind that we are not called upon to deal with legislation as though we were going to guess the outcome of any election.
I have no hesitation in saying that if, in the wisdom of the people of this country, we should be called upon to form the government, we would return to the supremacy of parliament, the rule of law and the federal system. There need be no doubt on that score. We will uphold the constitution; we will uphold the supremacy of parliament; we will uphold the rule of law and we will uphold the federal parliamentary democracy which is the special genius of Canada itself, the country which first gave that system to the world.
When we consider what we are going to do in connection with this act, let us remember that it is only by a discussion of this kind that we can clarify in the minds of the members, and in the minds of people beyond parliament itself, what the views of this parliament really are and what it is that this government and the supporters of this government are really seeking to do by the resolution now before us, and by the subsequent introduction of the bill when it comes before the house.
I have no intention of testing the tender sensibilities of those who are so concerned about any hint of lack of independence in their voting on the part of those who so regularly support this government. I only point out that in this particular case it is significant that once again there is that measure of unanimity that we see displayed so consistently whenever a measure of this kind is put forward. On other occasions we have heard member after member on the other side explain that they really believed in the resolution that was before the house, but that

they could not vote for it because in all conscience they could not vote against this government.
We heard that a few days ago; I need not mention the debate, because every hon. member will recall it. But once again this afternoon we had an hon. member seek to clear his own conscience by saying that he disliked this measure as much as anyone in this house, but he was going to vote for it because we were going to have an election inside of a year. It did not make any difference how bad the legislation was, he was going to continue it while this government was in power. That is a strange way of clearing one's conscience in regard to matters of this kind.
Now we are told that they are completely independent, and of course we must accept their statements. But it is interesting the way in which they assert their own belief in the very views we are putting forward, and then find some palatable excuse from their own point of view for deciding that they should not exercise that measure of independence which would certainly refresh so many Canadians at this time and restore their belief that members were voting exactly as they thought, without seeking to find some excuse for not doing so.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me what is most conspicuous in the views that have been expressed by those who seek to declare that it is expedient that we should extend this legislation is the apparent unconcern they display in regard to this challenge to our parliamentary system. If the regular procedure in parliament cannot operate now, at a time when we are called upon to sit in this house for eight or nine months a year, then when is it likely that we ever will be free again to exercise parliamentary freedom within the lifetime of any member of this house? This is the time for us to say that we believe we can operate our parliamentary system. At such time as there is any disturbance so affecting our systems of communication or transportation that the members of parliament could not be called quickly together, then and then only would it be time for us to pass legislation of this kind.
The Minister of Justice describes this as a twilight war. Mr. Chairman, the passing of legislation of this kind, when we have before us the judgment of the privy council in the Nolan case, which extends so far emergency authority of this kind, is indeed carrying us into the twilight zone; but it is not a twilight war. It is the twilight of democracy.
Emergency Powers Act
The hon. member for Nanaimo has referred to a book which it would be well for every hon. member to read. He has referred to the chapter in the book under the heading "The Road to Moscow". I have seen comments to the effect that it is inappropriate that anyone should draw any comparison here between the statements made in that very carefully written and objective book and the benign gentlemen who now make up this government. I remember the question:	Is it appropriate to speak about
"The Road to Moscow" when we look at the benign gentlemen who are administering our affairs at this time?
Well, you know, the strange part of it is that, so far as I have learned from the textbooks, the people now living in the countries beyond the iron curtain have exactly the same number of bones in their bodies, they have two eyes and two ears, a nose and a mouth and, except for their language or their statements, seem strangely like ourselves. And, in fact, they are strangely like ourselves, because many members in this house trace their ancestry back to the same blood as some of those who are now under communist slavery.
We must not for a moment think it is appropriate to change a system simply because we feel that those temporarily entrusted with the responsibility are benign gentlemen, unlikely to abuse the authority that would be conferred. Let us carry that one stage further, to a point that some may regard as carrying the argument to an absurdity, but which it seems to me does illustrate the point I would like to make. Supposing a government-I do not say this government-came before parliament and said that in view of the continuing emergency it was expedient that we should pass legislation which would suspend this parliament for a period of five years, is it thinkable that a single member in the house would say, "Oh, it is quite all right; let us do that".
To say that these benign gentlemen would not abuse their powers and would exercise the emergency powers given them in the intervening period in a way that would be perfectly satisfactory for the people of Canada, is not a sufficient answer. I can imagine someone saying, "But there is no similarity." Where is the dissimilarity? We are simply a parliament by tolerance under this act, that is all.
It is true that the government does not go so far as to say, as has been said under our system on an earlier occasion, "You can go home; you are no use here." The government does not say that in this case; but they do say by the act-whether they put it into words or not-"We ask you to trust us so
2114	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act completely that we want you to pass an act which, under the judgment in the Nolan case, we can exercise at any time to override the powers of every provincial legislature in this country, to withhold from parliament its ordinary responsibilities, and to deal with any aspect of the economic and personal life of the people of this country, subject only to the minor and relatively meaningless reservations contained in the act".
What is the difference? In one case we continue to meet and to discuss the matter. I agree there are some members who think we should not be discussing this subject. Only this afternoon the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) said, "We know what is going to happen. This thing will pass. The resolution will pass at this stage, and then the act will pass." And then a voice on the other side said, "Then what is the use of discussion?"
That is the attitude. They know it will pass, and they say, "What is the use of discussion?" Well, Mr. Chairman, meeting day by day and exchanging ideas as we do in our personal contacts, as well as in the house, it is difficult for many members to see the danger in the course they are being asked to follow.
We are not saying what this government will or will not do. We are simply saying that the government through this measure, under the decision in the Nolan case, is asking for dangerous and unparalleled authority which those who still respect the supremacy of parliament should not confer upon this or any other government in Canada.
If the statement made in the house this afternoon that "this is going to pass; why discuss it" were to be regarded as the views of hon. members generally, then I would recall the words of Cromwell when, upon dismissing parliament, he said there was nothing to be gained by keeping them there any longer, and that they could go home. If members on the other side of the house are simply to be counted as voting dummies, and if members on this side of the house are simply to be counted as those whose opinions should not be expressed because we must know that an overwhelming vote is going to support any proposition put forward by the government, then indeed we have come closer than anyone seems to realize to that day in Britain when for a time democracy was ended and a dictatorship was set up.

The laughter I hear from the member on the opposite side is the kind of laughter which it would be well for the people of this country to hear. I grant that


the member who laughed is not one of those members we would expect to understand a matter of this kind. In fact the hon. member who laughs has seen the consequences of the failure of those elected by the people to defend the rights of the people through their elected representatives. Nevertheless there are members in the house who have had occasion to study this matter.
That is what is before us here. What we are really being asked now is whether it is expedient that by legislation we should confer upon this government or any other government the right to by-pass the responsibility of the Commons and of parliament, and to override the rights and authority of the provincial legislatures under our constitution by perpetuating this measure for another year, and by that act invite the perpetuation of a system which is so contrary to the genius of our federal parliamentary democracy.
It is not for us to decide whether the Minister of Justice is right when he calls the present a period of twilight war. It is necessary for us to decide whether this is in fact a parliament which can be carried on as a free parliament under conditions which may be carried forward for a great many years.
We hope we do not face the prospects of another world war. We hope so with all our hearts; we hope it above everything else. We hope we will be able to preserve our freedom without another war; we hope we will be able to retain our parliamentary system for long years and keep the strength that comes alone from freedom, and through that strength build the combined power of free nations until at some time in the still distant future those countries now beyond the iron curtain shall assert their desires for their own systems of government, whatever those systems may be.
It will be recalled that there were many times during the great war when the parliament of the United Kingdom, from which we accepted the basic principles of our system, was called upon to meet under actual bombing or in uncomfortable places far removed from the ordinary associations of parliament. When future historians are examining the important events of the last war it may be that they will not point to Dunkirk or to El Alamein or to the invasion of Normandy or to the crossing of the Rhine as the great and outstanding event of the war which decided the course of free men and women throughout the years ahead. It may well be that historians examining what took place during the war will decide that the most important thing that happened was that in Great Britain, the home of our parliamentary system, although the House of Commons had

been bombed out, although for a time they met in an ordinary subway station, although they met under actual bombing, they never chose to abandon the supremacy of parliament or the rule of law.
It may well be that those who examine events from the distant and objective view of history will recall that at a time when London was under the heaviest bombing the British House of Commons sat for two days and discussed the freedom of men then held on the Isle of Man. London could be bombed, buildings could be destroyed, but the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament must be preserved at every expense. That may well be regarded as the most important thing because it stands before us today as an example that we should follow when conditions not only do not justify any argument for the abandonment of the supreme authority of this parliament, but demand an insistence upon the rule of law and respect of our federal system under our constitution.
We are in committee; members can ask questions and can express their views, but once again I urge the government-and I urge them in all earnestness-to reconsider their course, to remember that they have not put before us a single reason why it would be necessary to resort to the War Measures Act if this act were not passed. In fact everything that has been said shows that it would not be necessary to resort to the War Measures Act unless we were under the immediate threat of war and had difficulty in transportation and communication. That would be the only justification.
I also urge the government in all earnestness to recall that they have not shown us any reason why they need these wide powers. They have referred to the fact that last year they used the act so little that we need not be concerned about it. If they needed the act so little last year, why do they need these wide powers today?
Every argument put forward by the Minister of Justice is an argument which should, on reflection, impress upon the government the desirability of coming to this house and saying:	We have listened to
the arguments put forward; we do believe there is reason for the concern expressed; we do not accept these arguments as criticism of individuals now in office, but we have been impressed with the fact that any law now passed may affect those who will be called upon to assume responsibility at some future time, and we do not think we should pass on powers of this kind to another government because we sometimes have not indicated our confidence in others to do things as well as we do them.
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
Those who now argue that they have complete confidence in this government, if they still believe that Canada is a democracy and that the people of Canada are free to decide what government they will have, should be the ones to impress upon the government that consistent with the opinions they have expressed they should not pass on such wide powers because they might not be convinced that another government would be so all-wise, so omniscient as some of them seem to believe this government is.
I know some hon. members do not feel that we should be discussing this legislation at the length at which it has been discussed. That is what members of other parliaments have contended from time to time in the past. Without reflecting upon the motives of a single member of this government or of this house, it should be decided that it is not consistent with our federal parliamentary democratic system that at any time when parliament can easily be called together there should be handed to a government the power to declare by order in council that the rights of parliament or of provincial legislatures can be suspended in the way that can be done under this act.
Progress reported.
